title: Chapter 3
paragraphs: That the Division of Labor Is Limited by the Extent of the Market.

Since it is the ability to exchange that creates the opportunity for the division of labor, the extent of that division must always be limited by the extent of that ability to exchange—or, to put it another way, by the size of the market. When the market is very small, no one has any incentive to devote himself entirely to a single occupation, because he lacks the ability to trade the whole surplus of what his own labor produces, beyond what he himself consumes, for the parts of other men's labor that he needs.

There are certain kinds of work, even of the humblest sort, that can only be carried on in a large town. A porter, for instance, can find employment and a living nowhere else. A village is far too narrow a sphere for him; even an ordinary market town is barely large enough to keep him constantly occupied. In the isolated houses and tiny villages scattered across a region as empty as the Scottish Highlands, every farmer has to be his own family's butcher, baker, and brewer. In such places you can hardly expect to find even a smith, a carpenter, or a mason within twenty miles of another in the same trade. The scattered families living eight or ten miles from the nearest such worker must learn to do for themselves a great many small jobs that, in more populous countries, they would call in those tradesmen to do. Country workmen almost everywhere are forced to take on all the different branches of industry that are closely enough related to involve the same kind of materials. A country carpenter handles every sort of work made of wood; a country smith every sort made of iron. The carpenter is not only a carpenter, but a joiner, a cabinetmaker, even a wood-carver, as well as a wheelwright, a plow-wright, and a maker of carts and wagons. The smith's occupations are even more varied. It would be impossible for a trade as specialized as nail-making to exist in the remote, inland parts of the Scottish Highlands. Such a worker, making a thousand nails a day over three hundred working days a year, would produce three hundred thousand nails in a year. But in such a place it would be impossible to sell even a thousand—that is, a single day's work in the whole year. Because water transport opens a wider market to every kind of industry than land transport alone can provide, it is along the seacoast and the banks of navigable rivers that industry of every kind naturally begins to subdivide and improve itself, and often it is only a long time afterward that these improvements spread into the inland parts of the country. A broad-wheeled wagon, manned by two men and drawn by eight horses, carries and brings back nearly four tons of goods between London and Edinburgh in about six weeks. In roughly the same time a ship, crewed by six or eight men and sailing between the ports of London and Leith, frequently carries and brings back two hundred tons of goods. With the help of water transport, then, six or eight men can carry and bring back, in the same time, the same quantity of goods between London and Edinburgh as fifty broad-wheeled wagons manned by a hundred men and drawn by four hundred horses. So for two hundred tons of goods carried by the cheapest land transport from London to Edinburgh, one must charge the upkeep of a hundred men for three weeks, plus both the upkeep and the wear and tear—nearly equal to upkeep—of four hundred horses and fifty large wagons. For the same quantity of goods carried by water, one need charge only the upkeep of six or eight men, the wear and tear of a ship of two hundred tons' burden, and the value of the greater risk, or the difference in insurance between land and water transport. If there were no link between those two places except land transport, then, since no goods could be carried from one to the other except those whose price was very high in proportion to their weight, they could carry on only a small part of the trade that now exists between them, and consequently could give only a small part of the encouragement they now offer each other's industry. There could be little or no trade of any kind between the distant parts of the world. What goods could bear the cost of land transport between London and Calcutta? And even if any were precious enough to support that cost, how safely could they be carried through the territories of so many uncivilized nations? Yet those two cities now carry on a very considerable trade with each other, and by mutually providing a market, give a great deal of encouragement to each other's industry.

Since these are the advantages of water transport, it is natural that the first improvements in skill and industry should appear where this convenience opens the whole world as a market for the produce of every kind of labor, and that they should always be much slower to spread into the inland parts of the country. For a long time the inland regions can have no market for most of their goods except the country that surrounds them and separates them from the seacoast and the great navigable rivers. The extent of the market, therefore, must for a long time be proportional to the wealth and population of that surrounding country, and consequently their improvement must always come after the improvement of that country. In our North American colonies, the plantations have consistently followed either the seacoast or the banks of navigable rivers, and have scarcely anywhere spread any considerable distance from both.

The nations that, according to the most reliable history, appear to have been civilized first were those who lived around the coast of the Mediterranean Sea. That sea, by far the largest inlet known in the world, having no tides and therefore no waves except those raised by the wind alone, was extremely favorable to the world's infant navigation, thanks to the smoothness of its surface, the multitude of its islands, and the closeness of its neighboring shores—at a time when men, ignorant of the compass, were afraid to lose sight of the coast, and when the imperfect art of shipbuilding made them afraid to trust themselves to the rough waves of the open ocean. To pass beyond the Pillars of Hercules—that is, to sail out through the Strait of Gibraltar—was long regarded in the ancient world as a most remarkable and dangerous feat of navigation. It was late before even the Phoenicians and Carthaginians, the most skillful navigators and shipbuilders of those ancient times, attempted it; and for a long time they were the only nations that did.

Of all the countries on the coast of the Mediterranean Sea, Egypt seems to have been the first in which either agriculture or manufacturing was cultivated and improved to any considerable degree. Upper Egypt nowhere extends more than a few miles from the Nile, and in Lower Egypt that great river splits into many different canals, which—with a little help from human effort—seem to have provided a network of water transport not only between all the great towns, but between all the substantial villages, and even to many farmhouses in the countryside, much as the Rhine and the Meuse do in Holland today. The extent and ease of this inland navigation was probably one of the chief causes of Egypt's early development.

The improvements in agriculture and manufacturing likewise seem to have been very ancient in the provinces of Bengal in the East Indies, and in some of the eastern provinces of China, though the full antiquity of this is not confirmed by any histories whose authority we, in this part of the world, are well assured of. In Bengal, the Ganges and several other great rivers form a great many navigable canals, just as the Nile does in Egypt. In the eastern provinces of China, too, several great rivers form a multitude of canals through their different branches, and by connecting with one another provide an inland navigation far more extensive than that of either the Nile or the Ganges, or perhaps than both put together. It is striking that neither the ancient Egyptians, nor the Indians, nor the Chinese encouraged foreign trade, but all seem to have drawn their great wealth from this inland navigation.

All the inland parts of Africa, and all that part of Asia lying any considerable distance north of the Black and Caspian seas—ancient Scythia, modern Tartary and Siberia—seem in every age of the world to have been in the same uncivilized and barbarous state in which we find them today. The Sea of Tartary is the frozen ocean, which permits no navigation; and although some of the greatest rivers in the world run through that country, they are too far apart from one another to carry trade and communication through most of it. Africa has none of those great inlets—such as the Baltic and Adriatic in Europe, the Mediterranean and Black seas in both Europe and Asia, and the gulfs of Arabia, Persia, India, Bengal, and Siam in Asia—to carry maritime trade into the interior of that great continent; and the great rivers of Africa are too far apart from one another to give rise to any considerable inland navigation. Besides, the trade that any nation can carry on by means of a river that does not split into a great number of branches or canals, and that flows into another country before it reaches the sea, can never be very large, because the nations that hold that other territory always have it in their power to block the connection between the upper country and the sea. The navigation of the Danube is of very little use to the various states of Bavaria, Austria, and Hungary, compared with what it would be if any one of them controlled its whole course down to where it falls into the Black Sea.
